summary.text: Computing through the sixth term gives \(N=332572817028187686275682948600327513806149983112761\equiv3\pmod{18}\). Since \(19\mid171\) and \(2\) has order \(18\) modulo \(19\), \(2^N+1\equiv2^3+1=9\not\equiv0\pmod{19}\), so the required divisibility by \(171\) fails at the seventh step.

full_proof.text:
Let the sequence be defined by
\[
a(1)=a(2)=1,\qquad a(n)=\frac{2^{a(n-1)}+1}{a(n-2)}.
\]
We will show that the recurrence first fails to produce an integer at \(n=7\).

The first few terms follow directly from the recurrence:
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(3)&=\frac{2^{a(2)}+1}{a(1)}=\frac{2^1+1}{1}=3,\\
a(4)&=\frac{2^{a(3)}+1}{a(2)}=\frac{2^3+1}{1}=9,\\
a(5)&=\frac{2^{a(4)}+1}{a(3)}=\frac{2^9+1}{3}
      =\frac{513}{3}=171.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the next term is
\[
a(6)=\frac{2^{171}+1}{9}.
\]
Write
\[
N:=\frac{2^{171}+1}{9}.
\]
We first prove both that this quotient is an integer and that
\[
N\equiv 3\pmod {18}.
\]
For this purpose it suffices to calculate \(2^{171}\) modulo \(162=9\cdot18\).

We begin with
\[
2^9=512\equiv 26\pmod {162}.
\]
The following small reductions then give convenient higher powers:
\[
26^2=676=4\cdot162+28,
\]
so \(26^2\equiv28\pmod{162}\), and hence
\[
26^3\equiv28\cdot26=728=4\cdot162+80\equiv80\pmod{162}.
\]
It follows that
\[
2^{27}=(2^9)^3\equiv80\pmod{162}.
\]
Squaring this congruence gives
\[
2^{54}\equiv80^2=6400=39\cdot162+82\equiv82\pmod{162}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
82^2=6724=41\cdot162+82,
\]
so \(82^2\equiv82\pmod{162}\), and consequently \(82^3\equiv82\pmod{162}\). Therefore
\[
2^{162}=(2^{54})^3\equiv82^3\equiv82\pmod{162}.
\]
Using \(171=162+9\), we finally obtain
\[
2^{171}=2^{162}2^9\equiv82\cdot26=2132=13\cdot162+26
\equiv26\pmod{162}.
\]
Thus
\[
2^{171}+1\equiv27\pmod{162}.
\]
In particular, \(2^{171}+1\) is divisible by \(9\), so \(N\) is indeed an integer and the recurrence produces a legitimate integer sixth term. More precisely, there is an integer \(k\) such that
\[
2^{171}+1=27+162k=9(3+18k).
\]
Dividing by \(9\) yields
\[
N=3+18k,
\]
and hence
\[
N\equiv3\pmod{18}.
\]
(The exact value is
\[
N=332572817028187686275682948600327513806149983112761,
\]
but only its residue modulo \(18\) is needed.)

We now examine the proposed seventh term. Since \(a(5)=171\) and \(a(6)=N\), the recurrence would require
\[
a(7)=\frac{2^N+1}{171}.
\]
For this to be an integer, \(171\) would have to divide \(2^N+1\). We show that even the factor \(19\) of \(171=9\cdot19\) does not divide this numerator.

Modulo \(19\),
\[
2^9=512=26\cdot19+18\equiv-1\pmod{19}.
\]
Squaring gives
\[
2^{18}\equiv1\pmod{19}.
\]
Since \(N\equiv3\pmod{18}\), write \(N=18q+3\) for some nonnegative integer \(q\). Then
\[
2^N+1=2^{18q+3}+1=(2^{18})^q2^3+1.
\]
Reducing modulo \(19\), we get
\[
2^N+1\equiv1^q\cdot8+1=9\pmod{19}.
\]
This residue is nonzero modulo \(19\), so
\[
19\nmid 2^N+1.
\]
But if \(171\mid2^N+1\), then, because \(19\mid171\), transitivity of divisibility would imply \(19\mid2^N+1\), a contradiction. Hence
\[
171\nmid2^N+1.
\]
Therefore \((2^N+1)/171\), which is the expression prescribed for \(a(7)\), is not an integer. Thus not every term of the recurrence is an integer, and the conjecture is false.
